chapter_theme: The lament turns from the births endured to the Lord's neglect. After finishing the litany of sufferings (disease, deformity, weeping, Kama's arrows, Yama, Brahma's decree, Vishnu's discus, Rudra's destruction), the poet lists in a run of அையிலை (you did not) everything the Lord has failed to do: remove birth and death, burn the bond, give the ash, the rudraksha and the garb, call him into the devotees' company, grant release, silence and siddhi, fix him in stillness. He then asks for the side-glance of grace and, in a new run of பாரேனோ (shall I not see), begins to describe the Lord's form, feet, anklets, tiger skin, bull, elephant hide, deer and skull garland.
structure_note: Four runs: the close of the போதாதோ litany (459 to 465, now of sufferings rather than births); the ஐயிலை run of the Lord's omissions (465 to 475); a two-unit plea and set of questions (476 to 477); and the பாரேனோ run on the Lord's form, which continues through chapter 30 (478 to 483). The refrain stands as a separate line in 462, 466, 470, 474, 478 and 482.

459.reading: Are the days wasted and aching as disease ate me not enough? Are the days born as a ghost, for ghosts to eat, not enough?
459.nuance: பேயுண்ணப் பேயாய், born a ghost to be eaten by ghosts, adds the preta birth to the count of 454 to 458 and makes even that order prey to itself.

460.reading: Are the days got as a maimed body, hunched and blind, not enough? Are the days weakened by base food not enough?
460.nuance: ஈனப் புசிப்பு, mean eating, is either poor food or food got meanly; the count now runs through conditions within a human life rather than through births.

461.reading: Are the weariness suffered and the anguish not enough? Is it not enough that not even once was I asked 'ruined on your ruined day, were you?'
461.nuance: The second line is compressed: கெட்டநாள் கெட்டேன் என்று கேளாதும் seems to mean that no one so much as asked after him in his ruin, so the complaint is of being unregarded. The text's பட்ட களைப்பபும் has a doubled syllable.

462.reading: Are the days spent weeping over impermanence itself not enough? Are the days when all of them carried my burden not enough?
462.nuance: நில்லாமைக்கே அழுது may be weeping at impermanence or weeping only to no lasting purpose. என் பாரம் எடுத்த நாள், the day everyone lifted my burden, is most naturally the carrying of the corpse, so the second line is the poet's own funeral counted among his days.

463.reading: Is being brought to the end by Kama's arrows not enough? Is being struck four times by Yama's hand not enough?
463.nuance: கடைப்பட்டல் is to be reduced to the lowest or last state. நாலும் இடியுண்டல் may be four blows or 'even four'; the number is not explained. Kama and Yama, desire and death, are paired as the two assailants, as in 450 to 452.

464.reading: Is being cut to pieces by the four-faced one's written leaf not enough? Is being held fast in the discus of the one with honeyed tulasi not enough?
464.nuance: பட்டோலை, Brahma's written palm leaf, is the decree of fate written on the head. தேன்துளபத்தான் is Vishnu, and his நேமி (discus) stands for his office of preserving; தேக்குண்டல் (being dammed, stagnated) would then be the soul held in the round of sustained existence. 464 and 465 run the soul through the three gods' functions.

465.reading: Are the days met in Rudra's destruction not enough? You did not know my distress; you did not call me, saying 'come'.
465.nuance: The first line completes the triad (creation 464a, preservation 464b, destruction 465a), so the soul has been through all three acts. The second line begins the ஐயிலை run: the charge is now the Lord's own neglect.

466.reading: You did not end birth, you did not take me to follow behind you; you did not end death, you did not ask 'what is it?'
466.nuance: பின்னாகக் கொண்டையிலை, you did not take me behind you, is the image of the Lord walking with his servant following. The four complaints alternate the great (birth, death) with the intimate (following, being asked).

467.reading: You did not burn the bond; you did not end my anguish; you did not give the ash you wear, saying 'put it on'.
467.nuance: பாசம் எரித்தல், burning the bond, is Siddhanta's idiom for the removal of pasa. The ash is asked for as the Lord's own (பூசிய நீறு), given with the word புனை; what the poet wants is to be marked as his.

468.reading: You did not say 'servant'; you did not give the rudraksha bead; you did not give me your garb to look at the world as a thing to leave.
468.nuance: அக்கமணி is the rudraksha. The garb (வேடம்) is asked for with its purpose stated, விடும் உலகம் நோக்கி: the renouncer's dress is wanted as the means of seeing the world as something to leave, not as a sign for others. This is the garb Sivavakkiyar mocks (1188); Pattinathar begs for it.

469.reading: You did not call me into yourself; you did not make me one with you; you did not call me and set me in the company of your devotees.
469.nuance: ஒன்றாக்கிக் கொள்ளல், making one, is union; the devotees' company is set beside it as a second, humbler ask, and 470 lowers the request further still.

470.reading: You did not say 'here is one servant for us', a servant to the servants hidden in the high Supreme.
470.nuance: அடியார்க்கு அடியான், servant of the servants, is the Saiva formula of the lowest and surest place. ஓங்கு பரத்துள் ஒளித்த அடியார் are devotees hidden in the Supreme, so already released; the poet asks to be acknowledged as theirs. எமக்கென்று (for us) puts the words in the Lord's mouth.

471.reading: You did not have me bear the name; you did not stand so that 'I' ceased; you did not think of me in your protecting grace and call me.
471.nuance: நாமம் தரித்தல் may be bearing the Lord's name as a devotee's name or wearing his mark; நான் ஒழிய, with 'I' gone, is the ending of the ego that 449 showed refusing to forget itself.

472.reading: You did not give release; you did not give silence; you did not give siddhi; you did not take me up and cherish me.
472.nuance: Mukti, mauna and siddhi are listed as three gifts in one breath, with no ranking; சீராட்டுதல் is a mother's fondling of a child, the register the lament keeps turning to.

473.reading: You did not remove what hinders; you did not make me yourself; you did not end my desire, a fire that cannot be put out.
473.nuance: தவிர்ப்பைத் தவிர்த்தல், removing the removal, may mean removing the obstacle that keeps him off, or ending the Lord's own avoidance of him. அவிப்பரிய தீ, the fire hard to quench, answers the desires that spoke in 438 to 447.

474.reading: You did not fix me and keep me in the state of standing; you did not look so that the crowding inner organs perished all together.
474.nuance: நின்ற நிலை, the standing state, is the state of abiding, as tradition takes it; கரணம் are the inner organs (mind, intellect, will, ego) whose joint ceasing is the condition of it. பார்த்தல், looking, makes the Lord's glance the agent, which 476 then asks for by name.

475.reading: You did not look so that the bond of the bound world's spectacle fell away; you did not set me saying 'stand in nishtai'.
475.nuance: நிட்டை (nishtha) is fixed abiding, the yogi's settled absorption; the poet wants to be commanded into it, நில்லென்று. கட்ட உலகக் காட்சி, the world seen as a bound show, is maya as spectacle.

476.reading: Give the grace of your side-glance, Lord of Kannivanam; crush the impurity that ruins me and look so that I come near.
476.nuance: கடைக்கண் அருள், the grace of the corner of the eye, is the glance by which the Lord saves; the plea collapses the whole ஐயிலை list into one look. The verse names மலம் again, closing the frame opened at 435.

477.reading: Shall my longing not cool? Shall I not see and rejoice? Shall I not escape death? Shall my troubles not end?
477.nuance: காதல் is here the longing for the Lord, not the lust of 445; the four questions turn the complaint into hope, and the பாரேனோ run that follows answers 'shall I not see' at length.

478.reading: Shall I not praise you, shall I not come seeking your town, shall I not see your golden feet, shall I not stand filled?
478.nuance: ஊர் நாடி வருதல், coming in search of the Lord's town, is pilgrimage to the shrine of the refrain. பூரித்து நிற்றல், standing filled, is the state of the devotee before the image, and the word recurs as the poet's goal.

479.reading: Shall I not see the delight of the golden anklet that is Omkara? Shall I not see the fitting thandai and its many gems?
479.nuance: ஓங்காரப் பொற்சிலம்பு identifies the anklet's sound with Om, so the description of the form begins at the feet and makes the ornament a mantra. The run from here to 495 moves upward over the Lord's body in the order of a hymn of the form.

480.reading: Shall I not see the victory of the heroes' bell? Shall I not see that beauty which the ... praise?
480.nuance: வீரகண்டாமணி, the hero's bell, is worn on the leg as an emblem of valour; the Lord is pictured as a warrior. சூரர்கண்டி is unclear: it may be the brave ones who praise him, or a corruption of a word for the anklet-string. The reading of line 2 depends on it.

481.reading: Shall I not see the beauty of the tiger skin worn at the waist? Shall I not see the triumph of his coming mounted on the bull?
481.nuance: The tiger skin and the bull (விடை) are Siva's fixed iconography, so the Lord of Kannivanam is now described wholly as Siva. எழுந்தருளுதல் is the honorific for a deity's coming forth, as in a procession.

482.reading: Shall I not see the beauty of the elephant's hide he wore? Shall I not see the flower hand that holds the caught deer?
482.nuance: The elephant hide recalls the flaying of the demon Gajasura; the deer in the hand is the one sent by the sages of Daruka forest. The verse names the attributes and not the myths, as a hymn of the form does.

483.reading: Shall I not see the beauty of the chest hung with the heads of the dead? Shall I not wander crying 'he has taken us as his own'?
483.nuance: மாண்டார் தலை, the heads of the dead, is the skull garland. ஆண்டார் நமக்கு, 'he rules us' or 'he has made us his', is the devotee's cry of being taken into service; after the skulls, the poet's own wish is to be claimed.

links.note: Arunagirinathar blames deeds that the flower-born Brahma ordained for his failure to wear ash and say 'Hara Hara'; Pattinathar counts being cut up by Brahma's written leaf among what he has suffered, and three verses later complains that the Lord never gave him the ash.

Tirumular's Siva is the mad one who cuts off the births of those who renounce; Pattinathar's whole complaint assumes the same, that ending birth and death is the Lord's act to do, and charges him with not having done it.

Tirumular lists holy ash first among the emblems, then earrings and the rudraksha string, as the marks of the Siva-yogi; Pattinathar asks the Lord for exactly these, the ash in 467 and the rudraksha and garb in 468, as things to be given rather than put on.

Sivavakkiyar asks those who smear burnt ash and take up the garb in which of their mantras the Lord actually stirs, so the dress is an empty sign; Pattinathar begs the Lord to give him that very garb, as the means of seeing the world as a thing to leave. On the reading that Sivavakkiyar rejects the garb as such, and not only the garb without inner practice, the two cannot both hold.

Tirumular's flawless light took over his debts, made him stainless and gave his feet; Pattinathar asks for the same sequence in the imperative, the ruining impurity crushed and the Lord's look bringing him near.
The tiger skin, with the crescent and the ash, is what Tirumular's great love lies entwined with; Pattinathar's longing fastens on the same skin at the waist and asks whether he will not see it.

source_issues: 461 line 1 பட்ட களைப்பபும் has a doubled syllable, for களைப்பும்.
480 line 2 சூரர்கண்டி is obscure and may be corrupt.
The refrain கன்னிவனநாதா is printed as a separate line inside 462, 466, 470, 474, 478 and 482.
